m: A departure from what is normal or expected.
e: Latin aberrare, “to wander away”: ab- (away) + errare (to wander, stray). The same errare gives French errer and English err, error.
t: Picture a knight-errant drifting off the road: ab + errer = wandering off the normal path. French already has the word with the same meaning.

m: Bitter, sharp ill-feeling, especially in words or a dispute.
e: Latin acrimonia, “sharpness, pungency”, from acer (sharp, sour). Same root as French âcre, aigre and vinaigre (vin + aigre).
t: Acer → aigre → vinaigre. An acrimonious divorce is a marriage that has turned to vinegar.

m: A mixture or blend of different elements.
e: Medieval Latin amalgama, the alchemists’ word for an alloy of mercury with another metal, probably via Arabic from Greek malagma (a softening paste). Dentists’ silver fillings are still called amalgam.
t: Same word as « faire l’amalgame », lumping things together. Think of the dentist’s filling: several metals fused into one.

m: Open to more than one interpretation; unclear.
e: Latin ambiguus, “doubtful, shifting”, from ambigere, “to waver”: ambi- (both ways, around) + agere (to drive, lead).
t: Ambi = both ways, as in ambidextrous. A sentence driving in two directions at once. Identical to French ambigu.

m: Having mixed or contradictory feelings about something.
e: A modern coinage: the Swiss psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler built German Ambivalenz in 1910 from Latin ambi- (both) + valentia (strength, from valere, to be strong).
t: Ambi + valent = two feelings of equal strength pulling at once. Ambiguous describes a message; ambivalent describes how a person feels.

m: Willing to cooperate or be persuaded; open to.
e: Anglo-French amenable, “able to be led”, from amener (à + mener), from Late Latin minare, “to drive animals by shouting”. First a legal word: answerable to a court.
t: French amener: an amenable person is easy to « amener » to your view. You can lead them where you want.

m: Without a clear shape, form or structure.
e: Greek amorphos: a- (without) + morphē (shape, form). Same morphē as in metamorphosis and morphology.
t: A-morph = no shape, a metamorphosis that never finished. French « amorphe » often means listless; in English keep it about shape: an amorphous plan, an amorphous blob.

m: Deviating from what is standard or expected.
e: Greek anōmalos, “uneven, irregular”: an- (not) + homalos (even, level), related to homos (same).
t: An-homalos = not level, not the same as the rest. The anomaly is the data point that sticks out of the even line.

m: Cunning and sly (the usual GRE sense); also skilful.
e: English art + -ful. Art came through Old French from Latin ars, artis (skill, craft), which also gave artifice and artificial. “Skilful” slid to “crafty” by the 1700s.
t: Think artifice, not art gallery. The Artful Dodger in Oliver Twist is a pickpocket full of tricks.

m: Showing signs of future success; favourable.
e: Latin auspicium, “divination from birds”: avis (bird) + specere (to look). Roman augurs read the gods’ will in the flight of birds before any big decision.
f: favorable, de bon augure (« sous de bons auspices »)
t: « Sous de bons auspices »: picture the Roman priest watching the birds fly the right way. Auspicious = the birds say yes.

m: To give a false impression of; or to show something to be false.
e: Old English belēogan, “to deceive by lying”: be- + lēogan (to lie). Purely Germanic. The surface “lies about” what is underneath.
t: Be + lie: the surface tells a lie. “Her calm smile belied her panic” = the smile lied about it.

m: To reveal unintentionally (the GRE sense); also to be disloyal.
e: Germanic prefix be- + Middle English trayen, from Old French trair (now trahir), from Latin tradere, “to hand over”.
f: trahir (« sa voix trahissait sa nervosité »)
t: Exactly like French « trahir son émotion »: your face hands over (tradere) the secret without your permission.

m: A false statement made to damage someone’s reputation; slander.
e: Latin calumnia, “trickery, false accusation”, from calvi (to deceive). Came into English through French calomnie.
t: Same word as « calomnie », and the old saying: « Calomniez, calomniez, il en restera toujours quelque chose. »

m: To criticise or reprimand severely.
e: Latin castigare, “to correct, punish”, literally “to make pure”: castus (pure, chaste) + agere (to drive). The same verb became Old French chastier, now châtier, which English borrowed again as chastise.
t: Castigate and chastise are twins, both from castigare → châtier. « Qui aime bien châtie bien. »

m: Formal, severe disapproval; to criticise officially.
e: Latin censura, the office of the Roman censor (from censere, to assess). Censors ran the census and also judged citizens’ morals, publicly marking the disgraced.
t: Think « motion de censure » at the Assemblée: an official vote of disapproval. Censure = formal blame. Cutting out content is censor.

m: To scold or punish severely.
e: Middle English chastisen, from chasten, from Old French chastier (modern châtier), from Latin castigare, “to make pure”.
t: Chastise sounds like châtier because it is châtier. The twin of castigate.

m: In proportion to; corresponding in size or degree.
e: Late Latin commensuratus: com- (together) + mensurare (to measure), from mensura (measure).
f: proportionné à, à la mesure de
t: Com + mesure = measured together. “Salary commensurate with experience” = à la mesure de votre expérience.

m: To raise objections or show reluctance.
e: Old French demorer, “to linger, delay” (modern demeurer), from Latin demorari, from mora (delay, as in moratorium). Lawyers turned “delay” into a formal objection, the demurrer.
t: Demur = demeurer: you stay put instead of going along. Don’t confuse with demure (shy, modest).

m: Impartial, with no personal stake (not “uninterested”).
e: dis- (not) + interested, from Latin interesse, “to be between, to matter”: inter + esse. Here “interest” means a stake, as in conflict of interest.
t: Same as French « désintéressé »: a referee with nothing to gain. A disinterested judge is good; an uninterested judge is asleep.

m: Outstandingly bad; shocking.
e: Latin egregius, “standing out from the flock”: e/ex (out of) + grex, gregis (flock). It first meant “distinguished”; ironic use in the 1500s made the bad sense win.
f: flagrant, énorme, grossier (« une erreur grossière »)
t: Ex grege: the sheep that stands out of the flock, for the wrong reason. Same grex as gregarious and grégaire.

m: To weaken; drain of energy (not “to annoy” or “energise”).
e: Latin enervare, “to remove the sinews”: e- (out) + nervus (sinew, tendon). Old French énerver meant the same before it shifted to “irritate”.
t: Remember « les Énervés de Jumièges », the two princes of legend whose tendons were cut: énervés in the old sense, drained of strength. That is the English meaning.

m: Ambiguous, often deliberately; open to two readings.
e: Late Latin aequivocus, “of identical sound”: aequus (equal) + vox, vocis (voice). Two meanings with an equal voice.
t: Same as « équivoque »: two meanings speak equally loud, so you can’t tell which is meant. To equivocate = to dodge with double-meaning words.

m: Still in existence; surviving.
e: Latin exstantem, from exstare, “to stand out, be visible”: ex + stare (to stand).
t: Ex-stare = still standing. “The oldest extant manuscript” is the one still standing after the others were lost. Opposite: extinct.

m: Sparing and economical with money or food.
e: Latin frugalis, from frugi (useful, thrifty), from frux, frugis (fruit, produce). A frugal man made good use of his harvest.
t: Identical to « un repas frugal ». Frux = fruit: living on what your own trees give you.

m: To shock or excite someone into action.
e: Named after Luigi Galvani (1737–1798), the Bologna physician whose dissected frog legs twitched when touched with metals: “animal electricity”. The zinc-coating sense came later, from galvanic cells.
t: Picture Galvani’s frog leg jumping when the current hits it. To galvanize a team = jolt it into motion. Same in French.

m: Fond of company; sociable.
e: Latin gregarius, “of the flock”, from grex, gregis (flock, herd).
f: sociable, liant (« grégaire » is more pejorative)
t: Grex = the flock: a gregarious person loves being in the herd. In English it’s a compliment, unlike « l’instinct grégaire ».

m: A long, aggressive or pompous speech; to lecture forcefully.
e: Middle French harangue, from Old Italian aringa (public speech), from aringo (public square), from a Germanic word for a ring of people at an assembly (compare English ring).
t: Same as « haranguer la foule ». Picture a Germanic chief in the middle of a ring of warriors, shouting at them.

m: A person who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions.
e: Greek eikōn (image) + klastēs (breaker), from klan (to break). First the Byzantine iconoclasts of the 8th–9th centuries, who smashed religious images.
t: Icon-breaker: a monk smashing holy images. Today it’s someone smashing sacred ideas, like the founder who breaks every rule of an industry.

m: Rude, disrespectful; also (older sense) not relevant.
e: Latin impertinentem, “not belonging”: in- (not) + pertinere (to relate to). First “irrelevant”, then “meddling in what doesn’t concern you”, hence “rude”.
t: Both meanings come from “not pertinent”: either irrelevant, or poking into things that are none of your business.

m: Innocent, naive, candid (not “ingenious”).
e: Latin ingenuus, “native, freeborn”, hence “noble, frank”: in- + gignere (to beget). A freeborn person had nothing to hide.
t: Ingenuous = ingénu, like Voltaire’s L’Ingénu. Ingenious (with an i) is clever; disingenuous is fake-innocent.

m: Harmless; inoffensive.
e: Latin innocuus: in- (not) + nocuus (harmful), from nocere (to harm). Same family as French nuire, nocif and innocent.
t: In + nocif = not nocif. An innocuous remark does no harm at all.

m: To hint or suggest indirectly (the GRE verb sense).
e: Late Latin intimare, “to make known, announce”, from intimus (inmost): putting an idea into someone’s innermost thoughts.
t: The verb, said “inti-MATE”, slips an idea into someone’s mind without saying it. Not French « intimer un ordre », which is the opposite of subtle.

m: Complicated, intricate (the GRE sense).
e: Latin involvere, “to roll into, wrap up”: in- + volvere (to roll). Something rolled in many layers is hard to unwrap.
t: Picture a scroll rolled up on itself: an involved argument has to be unrolled layer by layer. Think « alambiqué ».

m: Using very few words; terse.
e: Greek Lakōnikos, “of Laconia”, the region around Sparta. Spartans were famous for blunt brevity.
t: Philip II of Macedon warned Sparta: “If I invade Laconia, I will destroy you.” The Spartans replied with one word: “If.”

m: To assert, claim firmly (the GRE sense).
e: Old French maintenir, from Latin manu tenere, “to hold in the hand”.
f: maintenir, affirmer, soutenir (« je maintiens que… »)
t: Exactly French « je maintiens que c’est faux »: you hold your position in your hand and won’t let go.

m: Subject to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood.
e: Latin mercurialis, “of Mercury”: the swift messenger god, the fast planet, and quicksilver, the liquid metal that never sits still. Astrologers said people born under Mercury were volatile.
t: Picture a drop of mercury (vif-argent) skittering across a table, impossible to pin down. A mercurial boss changes mood that fast.

m: Narrow in outlook; limited to local concerns.
e: Late Latin parochialis, from parochia (parish), from Greek paroikia: para (beside) + oikos (house). Thinking that stops at the parish boundary.
t: Parochial = paroissial. « L’esprit de clocher »: someone who can’t see past their own village church tower.

m: Extremely unwilling to spend money; stingy.
e: Latin parsimonia (thrift), from parcere, “to spare, save”.
t: « Avec parcimonie »: coins handed out one by one. Stronger than frugal: frugal is a virtue, parsimonious is stingy.

m: To speak evasively; to dodge the truth.
e: Latin praevaricari, “to walk crookedly, straddle”: prae + varicare (to straddle), from varus (bow-legged). In Roman law, a prosecutor secretly colluding with the defence.
t: Picture someone bow-legged, zig-zagging so they never walk straight to the truth. Tergiverser.

m: Wastefully extravagant; someone who squanders.
e: Latin prodigus (wasteful), from prodigere, “to drive away, squander”: pro- (forth) + agere (to drive).
t: The prodigal son of the parable, « l’enfant prodigue », who blew his inheritance. Not to be confused with prodigy (a genius).

m: Recklessly wasteful; also dissolute, immoral.
e: Latin profligatus, “ruined, dissolute”, from profligare, “to strike down”: pro- + fligere (to strike), as in inflict and conflict.
t: Profligate = prodigal who also parties. Pro + fligere: knocking down your own fortune and morals blow by blow.

m: To limit or modify a statement; add reservations (GRE sense).
e: Medieval Latin qualificare, “to give a quality to”: qualis (of what kind) + facere (to make).
t: Think « nuancer son propos ». A qualified endorsement is a yes with an asterisk.

m: Restless, impatient, resisting control.
e: Old French restif (now rétif), “stationary, balky”, from rester, Latin restare (to stay). Used first of horses that refused to go forward; their stamping and fidgeting took over the meaning.
t: Picture « un cheval rétif », refusing to move while stamping and pulling at the reins. A restive crowd is losing patience.

m: To weaken gradually or secretly.
e: Middle English under + mine (from Old French miner). Besiegers dug tunnels under castle walls, propped them with timber, then burned the props so the wall fell.
t: Same image as French « saper le moral »: digging under the wall until it collapses.

m: To scold or reproach severely.
e: Old English upbregdan, “to throw up against”: up + bregdan (to move quickly, weave; the source of braid). You throw someone’s faults back at them.
t: Up + braid: you hurl the reproach up into their face. It sounds harsh because it is.

m: Openness to bribery; corruption.
e: Latin venalis, “for sale”, from venum (sale), which also gave vendere, to sell (venum dare).
t: Think « la vénalité des offices » under the Ancien Régime, when judges bought their posts. Venal = for sale. Venial is a small, forgivable sin.

m: To regard with deep respect; revere.
e: Latin venerari, “to worship, revere”, related to Venus (love, desire).
t: Identical to « vénérer ». Picture bowing before a statue of Venus.

m: Truthful; accurate.
e: Latin verax, veracis (truthful), from verus (true).
t: Véracité = truthfulness. Don’t confuse with voracious (hungry): veracious = vrai.

m: To clear of blame; to prove right.
e: Latin vindicare, “to claim, avenge, set free”, from vindex (claimant, avenger). The same verb gave French venger and revendiquer.
t: Vindicate = venger: being proved right is your revenge. When the data vindicated her, she was avenged.

m: Lacking; not good enough.
e: Old Norse vanta, “to lack”, brought by Viking settlers. “Want” meant “lack” long before it meant “desire”.
t: From the Book of Daniel: “weighed in the balances, and found wanting” (« pesé dans la balance et trouvé léger »).
